sections.COMMENTS:
The Tell-Atlas system is an E-W striking, ca. 2,000 km-long contractional belt that runs along the southern coast of Western Mediterranean Sea from Morocco to Tunisia. The belt is formed by folds and thrusts generated by the continental collision between the African and Eurasian plates. A number of dextral strike-slip faults displace the folds and thrusts thereby creating a regional en-echelon pattern. On the basis of GPS measurements and focal mechanisms of earthquakes larger than 4.0 (Ml), Stich et al. (2006) have shown that part of the convergence is accommodated offshore. Near Algiers the shortening rate along a N10Â°W direction is of the order of 3.0 mm/yr on land and 1.5 mm/yr offshore (Stich et al., 2006).
The 2003, Mw 6.9, Boumerdes earthquake (located few kilometers off the Algerian coast) revealed unsuspected features of the Algerian margin, with strong implication for the seismic hazard of the region. All interpretative models for the Boumerdes earthquake require a south-dipping fault plane. Faults with this geometry were previously unknown in this region. Active faults mapped on land were all north-dipping thrusts. The Boumerdes fault seems to be part of an offshore system, capable of moderate-to-large earthquakes, which runs parallel to the Tell system. Deverchere et al. (2005) suggest that the offshore active faults are evidence of the ongoing underthrusting of the Neogene oceanic domain below the Algerian margin, which might represent an incipient stage of subduction.
The available focal mechanisms indicate dominant reverse faulting and a NNW-SSE regional maximum stress axis (Stich et al., 2006).
This Source is a portion of the offshore south-dipping thrust front located between Algiers and Bejaia. It is separated from adjacent portions by tearing structures due to the differential northward thrusting.
Seismicity generated by this seismogenic source during the instrumental period is essentially associated with the 2003 offshore Boumerdes sequence, with a mainshock of Mw 6.9 that represents the largest event known in the area. Other similarly large earthquakes are reported in catalogs on 11 May 1624 (Mw 6.7), 6 August 1912 (Mw 5.4), and 25 October 1949 (Mw 6.3).
We constrained the strike of the source taking into account the geometry of the known fault traces and the orientation of geologic and geomorphic features (Deverchere et al. 2005; Domzig et al, 2006). We determined the average dip and the rake of the source using the fault plane geometry from focal mechanisms and from other source models of the Boumerdes earthquake (Bounif et al. 2004; Meghraoui et al., 2004; Yelles et al., 2004; Semmane et al., 2005). The dip was constrained also based on seismotectonic cross-sections (Domzig et al., 2006). Even if most of these values were determined in the Boumerdes area, we assume them as representative of this seismogenic source also, for it belongs to the same regional geologic system.
We assigned to this source the slip rate values based on Kherroubi et al. (2009). These authors obtained these estimates from the shortening rate on the active folds imaged on seismic lines off Annaba.
Kherroubi et al. (2009) also inferred for the active faults near Annaba a possible maximum magnitude larger than 7 on the basis of the rupture length and average displacement they were able to detect on Chirp profiles.
sections.SUMMARIES:
Bounif et al. (2004)
The coastal mainshock of the 21 May 2003 Boumerdes earthquake was followed by a large number of aftershocks, the largest reaching Mw 5.8 on 27 May 2003. The authors investigated the mainshock, the first major aftershocks and about 900 smaller events recorded by temporary seismic stations using a master-event approach and the double difference (DD) method, thus providing accurate aftershock locations. The mainshock hypocenter was relocated using three major aftershocks (5.0<Mw<5.8) chosen as master events. The new mainshock location shifted on the coastline (36.83N, 3.65E) at 8-10 km depth. Earthquakes extended to about 16 km depth and delineate a N 55Â°-60Â°E trending and 45Â°-55Â° SE-dipping fault. It is the only significant events of the Tell Atlas of Algeria that was investigated in detail. Mainshock and aftershock relocations, the thrust focal mechanism (Harvard CMT: N 57Â°, 44Â°SE dip, 71Â° rake) and the seismic moment of 2.86*10EXP19 Nm together indicate that the earthquake source was a 50-km-long rupture that may appear at the sea floor 6 to 12 km off the coast into the Mediterranea Sea.
Meghraoui et al. (2004)
In this work the active deformation related to 21 May 2003 earthquake (Mw 6.9, northern Algeria) was modeled along the 55 km coastline between Boumerdes and Dellys, where coastal uplift marked by a continuous white band is visible. Most of measured points were collected using tape and differential GPS on rocky headlands. Leveling lines running parallel and orthogonal to the coast also provide the amount of uplift in the epicentral area. The uplift distribution shows an average 0.55 m along the shoreline with a maximum 0.75 m east of Boumerdes and a minimum close to 0 near Cap Djinet. The dislocation model predicts slip on a N 54Â°E trending reverse fault dipping 50Â°SE, in agreement with the CMT solution and with coastal uplift. The faulting characteristics imply a fault geometry with possible sea floor ruptures between 5 and 10 km offshore.
Deverchere et al. (2005)
The active seismogenic fault system in the area of the 2003 Mw 6.9 Boumerdes earthquake, Algeria was investigated through high-resolution swath bathymetry and a seismic survey. The results indicate that the two main slip patches of the 2003 Mw 6.9 Boumerdes earthquake are spatially correlated with two segmented cumulative scarps recognized on the slope and at the foot of the margin. The overall geometry indicates the predominance of back thrusts. The authors suggest that this implies underthrusting of the Neogene oceanic crust below the Algerian margin, which might represent an incipient stage of subduction.
Domzig et al. (2006)
In this work the authors present new results from the MARADJA 03 cruise, which investigated the offshore limit of the Internal Zones of the so-called AlKaPeCa domain using swath bathymetry and seismic reflection techiniques. Among other structures they identified slope breaks resulting from Plio-Quaternary activity of deep thrust ramps, one of them assumed to be connected at depth with the Boumerdes earthquake rupture. They conclude that the series of north-verging thrusts offshore Boumerdes are probably neoformed Plio-Quaternary structures and correspond to the beginning of the margin inversion.
Kherroubi et al. (2009)
These investigators describe for the first time a set of large active thrusts and folds near the foot of the easternmost Algerian margin, using swath bathymetry and high-resolution seismic data acquired during the Maradja2/Samra cruise. This active system forms a set of overlapping fault segments dipping toward the Algerian basin, in a way similar to what has been observed offshore to the east of Algiers on the rupture zone of 2003, Bourmedes, earthquake (Mw 6.9). Furthermore they estimate a horizontal shortening rate across large folds in the order of 1 mm/yr and hypothesize that these fault segments could have been responsible for large (M>7+) earthquakes in the past.
